Heinrich I von Müllenark (1190–1238) was the Archbishop of Cologne within the Holy Roman Empire from 1225 until 1237.

Born into a noble family, he rose through the ranks of the Catholic Church, serving as a canon in the Archbishopric of Mainz before being appointed Archbishop of Cologne.

During his tenure, Heinrich I von Müllenark played a significant role in the politics of the Holy Roman Empire, navigating the complex web of alliances and rivalries between the Emperor, the nobility, and the Church.

His legacy extends beyond his own time, as he laid the groundwork for the growth of the University of Cologne, one of the oldest universities in Europe.

Heinrich I von Müllenark's influence can be seen in the architectural legacy of the Cologne Cathedral, a testament to his commitment to the arts and his vision for a greater Christian unity.

Despite his passing in 1238, the impact of Heinrich I von Müllenark continues to be felt, as he remains a pivotal figure in the history of the Holy Roman Empire and the development of the Catholic Church in Europe.

The 14th-century chronicler, Jacob von Maursen, wrote of Heinrich I von Müllenark: 'He was a man of great piety, wisdom, and virtue, who served the Lord with great zeal and dedication.'

The legacy of Heinrich I von Müllenark can be seen in the lasting impact of the Cologne Dom on the city's architecture and cultural identity. His legacy also serves as a reminder of the complex and often tumultuous nature of medieval politics, where power and influence were constantly shifting and contested.


Despite his significant contributions to the history of the Holy Roman Empire, Heinrich I von Müllenark remains a somewhat obscure figure, overshadowed by more prominent historical figures of the time. However, his story serves as a testament to the enduring power of leadership and strategic thinking in shaping the course of human history.
